source_lines_after.27: Assume AC. For a finite tree $T$ the absolute bilinear tile contribution is $\le C\operatorname{density}(T)\operatorname{size}(T)|I_T|$, for $|g|\le\mathbf1_E$.
source_lines_after.37: [F4] The centered real-line maximal operator $M$ is bounded on $L^2$ [[cor-centered-hardy-littlewood-maximal-operator-is-l-p-bounded]].
source_lines_after.51: **Given:** A finite tree $T$ with designated top $t$, measurable selector $N$, $f\in L^2$, and measurable $g$ with $|g|\le\mathbf1_E$, $m(E)<\infty$. Put $J_0=I_t$, $L=|J_0|$, $\delta=\operatorname{dens}_{E,N}(T)$, $\sigma=\operatorname{size}_f(T)$ and $a_s=\langle f,\phi_s\rangle$. All constants depend only on the fixed packet.
source_lines_after.53: 1.1 The proof establishes the stronger sum of absolute tile contributions. Choose complex numbers $\varepsilon_s$ of modulus one so that $\varepsilon_sa_s\langle\mathbf1_{\omega_{s,+}}(N)\phi_s,g\rangle$ is nonnegative real, taking $\varepsilon_s=1$ for a zero product. Finite sesquilinearity bounds that sum by $\int_E|\sum_s\varepsilon_sa_s\mathbf1_{\omega_{s,+}}(N(x))\phi_s(x)|dx$. Write $b_s=\varepsilon_sa_s$. Empty $T$ and $\sigma=0$ give zero. If $\delta=0$, exponent $20$ packet decay bounds the integral of $|\phi_s|$ on $E\cap N^{-1}(\omega_{s,+})$ by $C\sqrt{|I_s|}\delta=0$ for each $s$, so all contributions vanish. Hence assume $\delta,\sigma>0$. Singletons give $|b_s|\le\sigma\sqrt{|I_s|}$. A possible member $s=t$ contributes at most $C\sigma L\int_{E\cap N^{-1}(\omega_t)}\chi_{J_0}\le C\sigma\delta L$, by packet decay with exponent $20$. Remove this one member. Each remaining tile has its top frequency contained in exactly one half of its frequency interval. Split them into the strict plus and strict minus trees according as that half is right or left, retaining the same top $t$ and the bounds $\delta,\sigma$. [F1, F2, F5, given]
source_lines_after.55: 1.2 We record a kernel bound. If $K_r$ satisfies $|K_r(z)|\le C r^{-1}(1+|z|/r)^{-20}$ and $h$ is Schwartz, then for every interval $J$ of length $j\le r$ and every $x,y\in J$, $|(K_r*h)(x)|\le C Mh(y)$. Indeed $|x-y|\le r$ makes the displayed weight at $x$ comparable to that at $y$. On $|z-y|<r$ its integral against $|h|$ is bounded by twice the centered average times a constant. On the annulus $2^nr\le|z-y|<2^{n+1}r$, it is at most $C2^{-19n}Mh(y)$, using the centered interval of radius $2^{n+1}r$. The geometric sum proves the bound uniformly in $x,y,r$. [F4]
source_lines_after.57: 2.1 For either nonempty strict subtree $U$, partition the line into maximal dyadic intervals $J$ such that $3J$ contains no $I_s$, $s\in U$; $3J$ denotes the concentric interval of triple length. Such intervals cover the line: all sufficiently small dyadic intervals have this property because $U$ is finite with positive minimum spatial length, and sufficiently large ancestors of any fixed interval fail it because their triples eventually contain every fixed bounded interval. The property passes to dyadic subintervals since their triples lie in the larger triple; maximal good intervals are therefore disjoint and cover every point. They form a countable family $\mathcal J$. If $j=|J|$ and $J^p$ is its dyadic parent, maximality supplies an $s'\in U$ with $I_{s'}\subseteq3J^p$. Since this latter interval has length $6j$, dyadic lengths imply $|I_{s'}|\le4j$. In particular $\operatorname{dist}(J,J_0)\le6j$. If $j\ge L$ and $J$ meets $J_0$, or if $j\ge L+\operatorname{dist}(J,J_0)$ when they are disjoint, then $J_0\subseteq3J$, contradicting goodness. Consequently intervals with $\operatorname{dist}(J,J_0)<L$ have $j<2L$ and lie in a fixed concentric enlargement of $J_0$; their total length is at most $CL$. When $d=\operatorname{dist}(J,J_0)\ge L$, one has $d/6\le j<d+L\le2d$. [F2, step 1.1]
source_lines_after.59: 2.2 For the strict plus subtree put $H=\sum_{s\in U}b_s\phi_s$, a Schwartz function. Then $\|H\|_2\le C\sigma\sqrt L$. Here are the needed orthogonality details. Lower frequency halves at unequal scales are disjoint: if nested, the full smaller frequency interval lies in the larger lower half, whereas the common top lies in its upper half. Plancherel kills those Gram entries. At equal frequency and spatial scale $l$, packet decay gives $|\langle\phi_s,\phi_{s'}\rangle|\le C(1+|c(I_s)-c(I_{s'})|/l)^{-20}$: extract the center-distance factor from the product of exponent $40$ decay bounds by the triangle inequality, and integrate the remaining normalized exponent $20$ weight, whose integral is $2/19$. The row and column sums over the length-$l$ spatial lattice are bounded by $C\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}(1+|n|)^{-20}$. Using $2|b_sb_{s'}|\le|b_s|^2+|b_{s'}|^2$ proves $\|H\|_2^2\le C\sum_s|b_s|^2\le C\sigma^2L$, the last bound being the defining plus-tree size inequality. [F1, F2, F3, F5, step 1.1]
source_lines_after.61: 3.1 On each $J$ split the signed tile sum into small tiles $|I_s|\le4j$ and large tiles $|I_s|\ge8j$. These are all the possibilities because lengths are dyadic. The integral of the absolute small sum is at most $$C\sigma\delta\sum_{s\in U:\,|I_s|\le4j}|I_s|\bigl(1+\operatorname{dist}(I_s,J)/|I_s|\bigr)^{-20}.$$ To see this for each tile of length $l$, exponent $40$ packet decay and the singleton bound give $|b_s\phi_s(x)|\le C\sigma l\chi_{I_s}(x)(1+|x-c(I_s)|/l)^{-20}$. Take the supremum of the last factor on $J$ and integrate over $E\cap N^{-1}(\omega_{s,+})$, a subset of the full-frequency set controlled by $\delta$. At a fixed scale $l$, there is at most one possible frequency for each spatial interval, the unique ancestor of the top frequency of length $1/l$. The spatial intervals thus form a subset of the length-$l$ dyadic lattice inside $J_0$. If $l\le j$, goodness and aligned dyadic endpoints put these intervals outside $3J$, at distance at least $j$ from $J$. Summing the displayed weights over that lattice gives at most $Cl\sum_{n\ge j/l}(1+n)^{-20}\le Cj(l/j)^{20}$ by integral comparison. For $l=2j$ or $4j$, the full lattice sum is at most $Cl\le Cj$, with no separation needed. Summing dyadic $l\le4j$ bounds the displayed spatial sum by $Cj$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1]
source_lines_after.63: 3.2 Let $G_J=E\cap J\cap\bigcup_{s\in U:\,|I_s|\ge8j}N^{-1}(\omega_{s,+})$, the support of the large sum on $E$. Then $m(G_J)\le C\delta j$. If there is no large tile the claim is immediate. Otherwise $8j\le L$. For the witness $s'$ in step 2.1, let $v$ have spatial interval the dyadic ancestor of $I_{s'}$ of length $4j$ and frequency the dyadic ancestor of the top frequency of length $1/(4j)$. Then $v$ is a tile above $s'$, so its weighted density integral is at most $\delta$. The center of its spatial interval is within $Cj$ of $J$, because $I_{s'}\subseteq3J^p$ and its ancestor has length $4j$. Hence $\chi_{I_v}\ge c/j$ on $J$ for an absolute $c>0$. Every large tile frequency is contained in $\omega_v$, since its length is at most $1/(8j)$ and it also contains the top frequency. This gives $G_J\subseteq E\cap J\cap N^{-1}(\omega_v)$ and proves the measure bound. Moreover $8j\le L$ and the witness geometry in step 2.1 place all such $J$ in one fixed enlargement of $J_0$. Thus their total length is at most $CL$ and $\sum_Jm(G_J)\le C\delta L$. The use of $4j$ for the density witness is essential: the witness in 3 times the parent need not have length at most $j$. [F1, F2, step 2.1]
source_lines_after.65: 3.3 We construct exact smooth scale projections for this plus subtree. For each dyadic $r\le L$, let $\Omega_r=[\alpha_r,\alpha_r+1/r)$ be the unique dyadic ancestor of the top frequency of length $1/r$. Set $\Theta(v)=\psi((v-1/2)/5)$. The exact plateau $a=1/9$ and support $b=1/8$ in F2 give $\Theta=1$ on $[0,1]$ and $\Theta=0$ outside $[-1/8,9/8]$. Its inverse Fourier transform is $k(x)=5e^{\pi ix}\phi(5x)$, as follows by substituting $v=5u+1/2$ in the absolutely convergent inverse integral. Thus the inverse transform of $\Theta(r(\xi-\alpha_r))$ is $K_r(x)=r^{-1}e^{2\pi i\alpha_rx}k(x/r)$, bounded by $Cr^{-1}(1+|x|/r)^{-20}$. For any member with $|I_s|\ge r$, its Fourier support lies in $\Omega_r$, so this multiplier is one on its support. If $|I_s|<r$, its full frequency is a proper ancestor of $\Omega_r$ and its lower packet support is separated from its upper half by at least $1/(8|I_s|)\ge1/(4r)$. Since the top, hence $\Omega_r$, lies in that upper half, the enlargement of $\Omega_r$ by $1/(8r)$ on each side misses that packet support. The multiplier is therefore zero there. By F6 and F7, $$K_r*H=\sum_{s\in U:\,|I_s|\ge r}b_s\phi_s$$ everywhere, not merely as an unspecified truncation estimate. [F2, F6, F7, step 2.2]
source_lines_after.67: 4.1 The small terms sum to at most $C\sigma\delta L$ over all $J$. For $\operatorname{dist}(J,J_0)<L$ this follows from the $Cj$ bound and the total-length bound in step 2.1. For $d=\operatorname{dist}(J,J_0)\ge L$, each scale $l\le L$ has total spatial length at most $L$, so its contribution to the spatial sum of step 3.1 is at most $L(1+d/l)^{-20}$. Summing the dyadic scales gives $CL(L/d)^{20}$. For $2^kL\le d<2^{k+1}L$, step 2.1 gives $j\ge2^kL/6$ and $j<2^{k+2}L$. The disjoint $J$ in this shell lie in an interval of length $C2^kL$, so their number is bounded by an absolute constant. Summing $CL2^{-20k}$ for $k\ge0$ completes the estimate. Countable sums of these nonnegative integrals are justified by F8 applied to finite unions of the disjoint $J$. [F8, step 2.1, step 3.1]
source_lines_after.69: 4.2 For each $x$, the upper frequency halves of a strict plus tree form a nested family, with all tiles at a fixed spatial scale having the same frequency. If $N(x)$ belongs to an upper half, it belongs to all the larger upper halves in this family. Thus the activated spatial scales form an initial segment of the scales present in $U$. Let $\tau(x)$ be their largest spatial length, setting it to zero when none is active. Every strict member has length at most $L/2$, so $2\tau(x)\le L$ whenever $\tau(x)>0$. On $J$, if $\tau(x)\ge8j$, the large sum equals the scale block $8j\le|I_s|\le\tau(x)$, which by step 3.3 is $((K_{8j}-K_{2\tau(x)})*H)(x)$. If $\tau(x)<8j$ the large sum is zero. Both kernel scales are at least $j$. Step 1.2 therefore bounds the magnitude of the large sum, for $x\in E\cap J$, by $C\mathbf1_{G_J}(x)\inf_{y\in J}MH(y)$. Denote that infimum by $q_J$; it is an ordinary fixed nonnegative number, not a measurability assertion about uncountably selected points. By F4 and step 3.2, $$\sum_Jm(G_J)q_J^2\le C\delta\sum_Jj q_J^2\le C\delta\int_{\mathbb R}(MH)^2\le C\delta\|H\|_2^2.$$ The middle inequality holds because $MH(y)\ge q_J$ on each disjoint $J$. Countable sums are again obtained from F8; alternatively the inequalities first hold for any finite subfamily. [F2, F4, F8, step 1.2, step 3.2, step 3.3]
source_lines_after.71: 5.1 For the strict minus subtree, upper frequency halves at unequal scales are disjoint. If two were nested, the full smaller interval would lie in the larger upper half, but the top frequency is required to lie in its lower half. At a fixed $x$, the selector $N(x)$ therefore activates at most one spatial scale. At that scale, $|b_s\phi_s(x)|\le C\sigma(1+|x-c(I_s)|/|I_s|)^{-20}$ and the sum over the spatial lattice is at most $C\sigma$, uniformly in $x$. The large sum on $J$ consequently has magnitude at most $C\sigma\mathbf1_{G_J}$ on $E$. Its integrals sum to $C\sigma\delta L$ by step 3.2. Together with step 4.1 this proves the bound for the minus subtree. [F2, step 1.1, step 4.1, step 3.2]
